nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Golden Age mystery and Albert Campion
literary_identity: Novelist; one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Albert Campion.
biography: Born Margery Louise Allingham in Ealing on 9 May 1904, the daughter of the writer Herbert Allingham; she published The White Cottage Mystery in 1928 and The Crime at Black Dudley, the first Campion novel, in 1929. Tiger in the Smoke (1952), The Tiger in the Smoke's predecessor The Fashion in Shrouds (1938) and The Beckoning Lady (1955) followed. She died at Colchester on 30 June 1966.
literary_profile: Margery Allingham was one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Albert Campion: her novels brought the thriller and the Dickensian character into the Golden Age mystery, and Tiger in the Smoke is one of the finest crime novels of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic detective and the grotesque villain; the London fog and the country house; the Dickensian minor character; the thriller plot inside the mystery; the plain, lively, inventive prose.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: Margery Allingham was one of the four Queens of Crime and the creator of Albert Campion: her novels brought the thriller and the Dickensian character into the Golden Age mystery, and Tiger in the Smoke is one of the finest crime novels of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the ten commandments of detection and the clerical wit
literary_identity: Priest, theologian and detective novelist; the author of the Decalogue of detective fiction and one of the founding wits of the Golden Age.
biography: Born Ronald Arbuthnott Knox at Kibworth, Leicestershire, on 17 February 1888; he was a fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, converted to Rome in 1917, and was the Catholic chaplain at Oxford from 1926. The Viaduct Murder (1925), The Three Taps (1927) and The Body in the Silo (1933) followed, with his translation of the Bible and his 'Detective Story Decalogue' of 1929.
literary_profile: Ronald Knox wrote the Decalogue of detective fiction, the fair-play rules that governed the Golden Age, and his own detective novels were among the wittiest of the period: his rules made the classical detective story a game with a code and his clerical wit gave the genre one of its founding critics.
stylistic_characteristics: The fair-play puzzle with its rules; the clerical detective and the Oxford setting; the learned joke and the paradox; the exact timetable and the map; the plain, witty, classical prose.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: Ronald Knox wrote the Decalogue of detective fiction, the fair-play rules that governed the Golden Age: his rules made the classical detective story a game with a code, and his own novels were among the wittiest of the period.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Hungarian-British; the historical adventure and the masked hero
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the creator of the Scarlet Pimpernel, the first masked hero of modern fiction.
biography: Born Emma Magdolna Rozalia Maria Jozefa Borbala Orczy in Hungary on 23 September 1865; her family moved to London in 1880, and she became a painter and writer. The Scarlet Pimpernel (1905), the play of 1903 and its many sequels made her famous. She died in Monte Carlo on 12 November 1947.
literary_profile: Baroness Orczy created the Scarlet Pimpernel, the first masked hero of modern fiction and the direct ancestor of Zorro, Batman and the superhero: her novel and play founded the double-life hero and the rescue narrative of the twentieth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-British; the spy novel and the Irish revolution
literary_identity: Writer and Irish nationalist; the author of The Riddle of the Sands, the first modern spy novel.
biography: Born Robert Erskine Childers in London on 25 June 1870; he served in the Boer War, wrote The Riddle of the Sands in 1903, ran guns to Ireland in the Asgard in 1914, and became a minister in the Irish Free State. He was executed by the Free State government on 24 November 1922.
literary_profile: Erskine Childers wrote The Riddle of the Sands, the first modern spy novel and the founding text of the genre: its sailing, its German invasion plot and its factual exactness created the espionage novel and made the threat of war the subject of popular fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The yachting narrative and the exact seamanship; the documentary detail of the Frisian coast; the amateur spy and the discovery; the plain, factual, reportorial prose; the invasion plot that made the novel a warning.
intellectual_concerns: Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; the First World War and the myth of sacrifice; totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel.
historical_significance: Erskine Childers wrote The Riddle of the Sands, the first modern spy novel and the founding text of the genre: its sailing, its German invasion plot and its factual exactness created the espionage novel and made the threat of war the subject of popular fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the smuggling romance and the antiquarian ghost story
literary_identity: Novelist and antiquarian; the author of Moonfleet, one of the great English adventure novels.
biography: Born John Meade Falkner at Manningford Bruce, Wiltshire, on 8 May 1858; he was a schoolmaster and then a director of Armstrong Whitworth, and published The Lost Stradivarius (1895), Moonfleet (1898) and The Nebuly Coat (1903). He was honorary librarian to the Dean and Chapter of Durham and died at Burford on 22 July 1932.

stylistic_characteristics: The first-person Dorset narrative of the boy smuggler; the underground vault and the diamond; the antiquarian ghost story of the Stradivarius; the architectural detail of the cathedral; the plain, exact, old-fashioned prose.
intellectual_concerns: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the supernatural and the antiquarian; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination.
historical_significance: John Meade Falkner wrote Moonfleet, one of the great English adventure novels and the finest smuggling romance in the language: The Lost Stradivarius is one of the finest antiquarian ghost stories of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Italian-British; the swashbuckler and the historical romance
literary_identity: Novelist; the greatest writer of the swashbuckling historical romance in English.
biography: Born Rafael Sabatini at Jesi, Italy, on 29 April 1875 to an Italian father and an English mother; he grew up in Portugal and Switzerland and settled in England, publishing The Sea-Hawk (1915), Scaramouche (1921) and Captain Blood (1922). He died at Adelboden, Switzerland, on 13 February 1950.

literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Beau Geste, the most famous French Foreign Legion novel in English.
biography: Born Percival Christopher Wren at Devizes, Wiltshire, on 1 November 1875; he served in India and with the French Foreign Legion, and published Beau Geste in 1924, followed by Beau Sabreur (1926), Beau Ideal (1928) and some thirty other novels. He died at Amberley, Gloucestershire, on 22 November 1941.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comic novel and the Scottish island
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and nationalist; the author of Whisky Galore and Sinister Street, and a central figure of the Scottish Renaissance.
biography: Born Edward Montague Compton Mackenzie at West Hartlepool on 17 January 1883; he was educated at Oxford, published Sinister Street (1913–14) and Youth's Encounter (1913), served in the Aegean in the First World War, and founded the Scottish National Party's predecessor. Whisky Galore (1947), The Monarch of the Glen (1941) and The Four Winds of Love followed, and he died in Edinburgh on 30 November 1972.

stylistic_characteristics: The comic novel of the island; the exact topography of the Hebrides; the dialogue of the islanders; the society comedy of the metropolis; the plain, warm, discursive prose.
